MAPThe precursor ladder: size of the clone, then damage

LO 1Normal immunoglobulin production

Q1. How does a B cell become an Ig-secreting plasma cell?
  1. Naïve B cell meets antigen → germinal center with T follicular helper cells (CD4+, PD-1+)
  2. Proliferation, somatic hypermutation, class switching
  3. → memory B cell or long-lived plasma cell that homes to the marrow
  • Plasma cell = terminally differentiated B cell: eccentric "clock-face" nucleus, blue cytoplasm, pale perinuclear hof (Golgi)

Plasma cells

  • Eccentric nucleus, hof

Ig structure

  • 2 heavy + 2 light chains
Q2. How is an immunoglobulin built?
  • 2 identical heavy + 2 identical light chains; variable + constant regions
  • Light chain = κ or λ, never both
  • Each clone makes one heavy + one light chain for life, plus a slight excess of light chains (small amounts normally in urine)
Heavy chainClassForm
γIgGMonomer (most myelomas)
αIgADimer (can thicken blood)
μIgMPentamer → hyperviscosity (Waldenström)
δ, εIgD, IgEMonomers (rare myelomas)
Q3. What is the difference between polyclonal and monoclonal?

Polyclonal (normal / reactive)

  • Thousands of clones → broad γ band
  • Both κ and λ plasma cells (~2:1)

Monoclonal (neoplasm)

  • One clone → one product (M protein) → tall narrow spike
  • Light-chain restriction: far more κ than λ (or vice versa)

Reactive: κ

  • κ cells present

Reactive: λ

  • λ cells also present → polyclonal

Myeloma: κ

  • Sheets of κ+ cells

Myeloma: λ

  • λ negative → κ-restricted
In-house exam

Plasma cells with κ and λ = reactive (polyclonal). Mostly κ (or λ) = monoclonal → neoplasm.

Analogy — the choir

Normal immunity is thousands of voices (a broad hum). In myeloma one singer grabs the microphone: one loud note (M spike) while the rest go quiet (↓ normal Igs → infections).

LO 2Classifying plasma cell neoplasms

Q1. What does the WHO classification include?
CategoryEntities
PrecursorsNon-IgM MGUS (→ myeloma or AL amyloid, ~1%/y) · IgM MGUS (→ Waldenström, ~1.5%/y)
Plasma cell myelomaMultiple myeloma
Myeloma variantsSmoldering · non-secretory · plasma cell leukemia
PlasmacytomaSolitary plasmacytoma of bone · extraosseous
Ig deposition diseasesPrimary (AL) amyloidosis · light/heavy chain deposition disease
ParaneoplasticPOEMS · TEMPI · AESOP
B-cell lymphoma with plasma cell differentiationLymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström) · heavy chain diseases
Q2. How do MGUS, smoldering and active myeloma differ?
MGUSSmolderingMultiple myeloma
Serum M protein<3 g/dL≥3 g/dL (or urine M >500 mg/24 h)Any (usually high)
Clonal marrow PCs<10%10–59%≥10% or plasmacytoma
CRAB / SLiMNoneNone≥1 present
Course~1%/y (≈20% over 10–15 y)Higher risk; ~10-y survivalTreat
  • MGUS: ~3% of adults over 50; most myelomas start here
  • MGUS risk factors: abnormal FLC ratio, IgA or IgM type, M protein >1.5 g/dL (all 3 → 50–60% progression at 20 y; none → 5%)
Trap

Smoldering myeloma carries a higher progression risk than MGUS, not lower. And ≥10% clonal plasma cells alone isn't myeloma: WHO also needs a myeloma-defining event, otherwise it's smoldering.

Q3. What are the other plasma cell disorders?
DisorderKey features
Solitary plasmacytomaOne mass of clonal plasma cells, marrow normal, no CRAB. Bone (thoracic vertebra) → ~50% progress to myeloma; extraosseous (head/neck 90%) → ~15%. Treat with radiation
AL amyloidosisMisfolded light chains (usually λ) deposit: nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy, macroglossia, neuropathy, periorbital purpura; Congo red apple-green birefringence
POEMSPolyneuropathy · Organomegaly · Endocrinopathy · M protein (usually λ) · Skin changes; ↑ VEGF; sclerotic bone lesions
Light-chain myeloma~20%: only light chains → no serum spike, Bence Jones proteinuria, worse kidneys
Non-secretory / plasma cell leukemiaRare variants; PCL is aggressive
In-house exam

Know POEMS: polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M protein, skin changes.

Step 1

AL (light chain) vs AA amyloid: AA follows chronic inflammation and has no M protein. Both: Congo red, apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A 48-year-old has an IgG κ spike of 2.1 g/dL, 4% marrow plasma cells and normal calcium, creatinine, hemoglobin and bones. Diagnosis?
MGUS: observe.
A2A new patient has 65% clonal marrow plasma cells but normal calcium, creatinine, hemoglobin and bones. Smoldering or active?
Active myeloma: ≥60% is a SLiM myeloma-defining event.

LO 3The M protein and how to find it

Q1. Which tests find and type the M protein?
TestWhat it doesKey point
Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)Proteins separate: albumin, α1, α2, β, γ; a monoclonal protein runs to one spot → M spikeScreens + quantifies; use serum (no fibrinogen peak)
ImmunofixationAntisera to γ, α, μ, κ, λTypes the spike (e.g., IgG κ)
24-h urine electrophoresisDetects free light chains = Bence Jones proteinOften only light chains in urine
Serum free light chainsFree κ and λAbnormal κ:λ = clonal; involved/uninvolved >100 = myeloma-defining

Normal SPEP

  • Albumin + small humps

M spike

  • Albumin + narrow γ spike
In-house exam

Abnormal SPEP shows two peaks: albumin + the M spike.

Step 1 — workup order

SPEP (find) → immunofixation (type) → UPEP/FLC (light chains) → marrow biopsy (% clonal PCs, FISH) → skeletal imaging. Classic labs: ↑ total protein with normal/↓ albumin (protein gap), rouleaux, ↑ ESR, low anion gap.

Trap — no serum spike ≠ no myeloma

Light-chain myeloma (~20%) makes only light chains, which are filtered into urine: SPEP shows hypogammaglobulinemia. Urine dipstick detects albumin, not light chains; use UPEP or serum FLC.

LO 4Multiple myeloma

Q1. What is myeloma, who gets it and why?
  • Marrow-based, multifocal neoplasm of clonal plasma cells with end-organ damage
  • Median age 70; men; ~2× more common in Black patients; ~1% of cancers, 15% of heme cancers
  • Risks: pesticides, asbestos, petroleum, radiation, chronic antigen stimulation
  • Post-germinal center B → plasma cell; grows on IL-6 and IL-10 (high IL-6 = poor prognosis)
  • M protein: IgG 55%, IgA 20%, light chain ~20%, IgD 2%, non-secretory 1%; κ > λ
Q2. Why do bones, blood and kidneys fail?
Memory tool — CRAB

Calcium ↑ · Renal failure · Anemia · Bone lesions (+ infection).

Trap — bone scan and ALP

Pure bone destruction with suppressed osteoblasts → bone scan negative, alkaline phosphatase usually normal. Use X-ray, CT, MRI or PET.

Q3. What does myeloma look like on imaging and in the marrow?
  • X-ray: punched-out lytic lesions (skull, ribs, vertebrae) in ~80%; fractures
  • Marrow: ≥10% clonal plasma cells in sheets/clusters; binucleate cells; Mott cells / Russell bodies; high N:C ratio = worse
  • Blood: rouleaux (high Ig neutralizes RBC charge) and ↑ ESR
  • Markers: CD38, CD138, cytoplasmic Ig; CD19, CD27, CD81 lost; CD56+; CD45 dim

Punched-out skull

  • Lytic lesions, no sclerotic rim

Myeloma marrow

  • Sheets of plasma cells

Rouleaux

  • RBCs stacked like coins

Mott cell

  • Cytoplasmic Ig globules (Russell bodies)
In-house exam
  • Punched-out skull lesions → myeloma
  • Myeloma cells: CD38, CD138, cytoplasmic Ig; no CD19, CD27, CD81
  • Rouleaux = high Ig
  • ≥10% clonal plasma cells (+ a defining event)
Q4. How does myeloma present?
  • Bone pain, pathologic fractures (vertebra), cord compression
  • Anemia, fatigue
  • Recurrent infections (encapsulated bacteria)
  • Hypercalcemia: confusion, weakness, constipation
  • Renal failure: cast nephropathy (light chains + Tamm-Horsfall), hypercalcemia, amyloid
  • Physical exam often normal
Step 1

Kidney biopsy with large fractured casts in distal tubules and giant cells → myeloma cast nephropathy. Heavy albuminuria in myeloma → think AL amyloid.

Q5. What are the diagnostic criteria, lab tests and cytogenetics?

WHO: clonal marrow PCs ≥10% (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) + ≥1 of:

CRAB

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Anemia
  • ≥1 bone lesion (X-ray, CT, PET/CT)

SLiM

  • Sixty: ≥60% clonal PCs
  • Light chain ratio >100
  • MRI: >1 focal lesion
RiskAbnormalityPartner
FavorableHyperdiploidyOdd-numbered trisomies
Favorablet(11;14), t(6;14)Cyclin D1, D3
Unfavorablet(4;14), t(14;16), t(14;20)FGFR3/MMSET, c-MAF, MAFB → cyclin D2
Unfavorabledel(17p13)TP53
Unfavorabledel 13 / monosomy 13 (~50%); hypodiploidy; 1p del, 1q21 gain—
  • Abnormalities seen in ~30% by karyotype but ~90% by FISH (plasma cells divide slowly)
  • IGH (14q32) translocations 55–70%; KRAS/NRAS 30–40%
Memory tool

"SLiM CRAB": any of these = treat. Cyclin D1/D3 good, D2 bad; "4-16-20 are bad numbers."

In-house exam

Most common myeloma chromosome change: monosomy / partial deletion of 13.

Trap

t(11;14) is favorable in myeloma but defines mantle cell lymphoma.

Q6. What predicts outcome?
ISS stageCriteriaMedian survival
Iβ2-microglobulin <3.5 mg/L + albumin ≥3.5 g/dL62 mo
IINeither I nor III44 mo
IIIβ2-microglobulin ≥5.5 mg/L29 mo
  • Poor prognosis: high stage, low Hb, high Ca, renal dysfunction, extensive lytic lesions, plasmablastic morphology, high-risk FISH, ↑ IL-6, circulating plasma cells, minimal residual disease
  • Incurable; death from infection, renal failure
  • MRD monitoring, least → most sensitive: morphology → flow → FISH → molecular (PCR/NGS)
Q7. How is myeloma treated?
ClassExamples · mechanism
TraditionalMelphalan + prednisone (oral)
Proteasome inhibitorsBortezomib: misfolded Ig piles up → ER stress, apoptosis; ↓ NF-κB. Neuropathy, zoster
IMiDsThalidomide, lenalidomide: anti-angiogenic, immune; teratogenic, VTE
AntibodiesDaratumumab (anti-CD38) · elotuzumab (anti-SLAMF7)
BoneBisphosphonates, denosumab (inhibit resorption)
TransplantAutologous stem cell transplant after conditioning, usually younger/fit patients
Step 1

Plasma cells make huge amounts of protein, so blocking the proteasome kills them first. Daratumumab can make myeloma cells look CD38-negative on flow.

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A 61-year-old man has 5 months of back pain, pneumococcal pneumonia, creatinine 3.7 and punched-out skull lesions. What will the marrow show?
Sheets of atypical clonal plasma cells (≥10%), CD38/CD138+.
A2A 70-year-old with back pain and creatinine 2.9 has no serum M spike. What's the likely diagnosis and test?
Light-chain myeloma: UPEP (Bence Jones protein) or serum free light chains.

LO 5Waldenström macroglobulinemia

Q1. What are the clinical and pathologic features?
  • Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma + IgM M protein; median age 63, men; precursor = IgM MGUS; hepatitis C association
  • B lymphocytes → plasmacytoid lymphocytes → plasma cells; MYD88 L265P (~90%; → NF-κB); CXCR4 predicts response
  • Fatigue, weight loss; marrow failure (anemia, infection, bleeding); nodes, spleen
  • Hyperviscosity (10–30%): blurred vision, "sausage-link" retinal veins, headache, stroke, mucosal bleeding, neuropathy
  • Cryoglobulinemia (Raynaud), cold agglutinins; Bing-Neel (CNS)
  • No lytic lesions, no hypercalcemia
High yield — why IgM thickens blood

IgM is a pentamer (~900 kDa) that stays in vessels → sludging, rouleaux, hyperviscosity. Treat urgently with plasmapheresis.

Q2. What does the marrow show?
  • Mix of small lymphocytes, plasmacytoid lymphocytes and plasma cells
  • Dutcher bodies (intranuclear Ig inclusions)
  • Increased mast cells

Lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate

  • Lymphocytes → plasma cells

Plasmacytoid cells

  • Lymphocytes with plasma cell features

Mast cell

  • ↑ in Waldenström marrow
In-house exam

Mast cells in a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate → lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Dutcher bodies → Waldenström; Russell bodies → myeloma.

Q3. Which tests make the diagnosis?
  • SPEP → IgM on immunofixation (usually κ)
  • Marrow, nodes, blood: lymphoplasmacytic cells; CD19, CD20+, surface IgM; CD5−, CD10−
  • MYD88 L265P testing
  • Marked rouleaux, ↑ ESR; serum viscosity; keep samples warm (cryoglobulins)

IgM spike

  • Typed by immunofixation
Q4. How is Waldenström different from myeloma and other lymphomas?
WaldenströmMyeloma
M proteinIgMIgG > IgA, light chain
CellsLymphocytes → plasmacytoid → plasma cellsPure plasma cells
MarkersCD20+, sIgMCD38, CD138; CD19/20−
BoneNo lytic lesions, no hypercalcemiaLytic lesions, hypercalcemia
Nodes / spleenYesUnusual
InclusionsDutcher bodies, mast cellsRussell bodies / Mott cells
MutationMYD88 L265PNot MYD88
BothM spike, anemia, rouleaux, possible hyperviscosity
  • vs CLL (CD5/CD23+), mantle (CD5, cyclin D1), follicular (CD10)
  • Course: indolent, median ~4–7 y; rarely → DLBCL; poor: age, cytopenias, neuropathy, weight loss
  • Treatment: alkylators or steroids ± rituximab, BTK inhibitors; hyperviscosity → plasmapheresis
In-house exam

M spike with no lytic lesions or hypercalcemia → Waldenström, not myeloma.

Memory tool

Waldenström = "thick blood, no holes": IgM pentamer, CD20, Dutcher bodies, mast cells.

ApplyLO 5 application question

A1A 67-year-old man has blurred vision, nosebleeds, lymphadenopathy and sausage-link retinal veins; skeletal survey is normal. Diagnosis, mutation and urgent treatment?
Waldenström; MYD88 L265P; plasmapheresis for hyperviscosity.

IDImage ID

Image 1 — electrophoresis
Albumin + M spike → monoclonal gammopathy.
Image 2 — X-ray
Punched-out lytic lesions → myeloma.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A marrow biopsy shows increased plasma cells; IHC shows both κ- and λ-positive cells in about a 2:1 ratio. Interpretation?

No light-chain restriction.

2A 69-year-old woman has back pain, a T10 compression fracture and multiple lytic lesions. Marrow aspirate shows plasma cells. Which lab finding is most likely?

Light chains in urine; bone scan and ALP usually normal.

3Which immunophenotype fits myeloma cells?

Also CD27/CD81 lost; CD56+.

4A 66-year-old has an IgG spike of 3.8 g/dL and 22% marrow plasma cells; calcium, creatinine, hemoglobin and MRI are normal; FLC ratio is 20. Diagnosis?

≥3 g/dL and 10–59% PCs without CRAB or SLiM.

5Which mediator from marrow stroma drives osteoclast activation and lytic lesions in myeloma?

With IL-1β, IL-6, TNF.

6A patient with confusion, constipation and calcium of 13.8 mg/dL has rouleaux on the smear. Most likely underlying disease?

Hypercalcemia + rouleaux; Waldenström lacks hypercalcemia.

7Which is the most common cytogenetic abnormality in myeloma?

~50%; best seen by FISH.

8Two myeloma patients have FISH results: A has t(11;14); B has t(4;14) and del(17p). Which statement is correct?

Cyclin D1 good; 4-16-20 and 17p bad.

9A patient has polyneuropathy, hepatosplenomegaly, hypothyroidism, a λ M protein and skin hyperpigmentation. Diagnosis?

Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M protein, Skin.

10A myeloma patient develops heavy albuminuria, macroglossia and a stiff, restrictive heart. Biopsy will show:

AL amyloidosis (usually λ).

11A 67-year-old has blurred vision, epistaxis, lymphadenopathy, an IgM spike and a normal skeletal survey. Which finding is expected in the marrow?

Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma.

12Which mutation is found in ~90% of Waldenström but not in myeloma?

Activates NF-κB.

13Bortezomib kills myeloma cells mainly by:

ER stress → apoptosis; ↓ NF-κB. Side effects: neuropathy, zoster.
